artiest/tristan-murail.text:
Tristan Murail was born in Le Havre in 1947. He first studied political science and economics and learned to play the ondes Martenot. This brought him into contact with Jeanne Loriod and her brother-in-law Olivier Messiaen, with whom he studied composition at the Paris Conservatoire from 1967 to 1972. In 1971 he won the Prix de Rome. Two years later he co-founded Ensemble l'Itinéraire. From 1991 to 1997 he taught computer music and composition at IRCAM in Paris and helped develop the composition software Patchwork. After that he was a professor at Columbia University in New York until 2010.

Murail belongs to spectral music. This approach takes the natural properties of sound as the basis for harmony and derives chords and polyphony from sound analysis and electronic synthesis. His best-known works include Gondwana from 1980, Désintégrations for seventeen instruments and tape from 1982, Time and Again from 1985 and Serendib from 1992. He wrote Treize couleurs du soleil couchant for ensemble in 1978. Vampyr! is a rare classical piece for electric guitar, in which he refers to rock guitarists such as Carlos Santana and Eric Clapton.

Murail shows how close the classical avant-garde and the world of synthesizers and recording studios could come to one another. His way of thinking about timbre continues to resonate in a great deal of contemporary music.
artiest/tristan-murail.listen: Listen to Treize couleurs du soleil couchant and notice how the sound slowly changes colour, as if the light were shifting. Try to hear which sounds linger and which fade away.

artiest/tristram-cary.text:
Tristram Cary was an English-Australian composer and a pioneer of electronic music. He was born in Oxford in 1925, the son of the writer Joyce Cary. As a radar engineer in the Royal Navy during the Second World War, he developed his own ideas about electronic music and tape music independently. After the war he built one of the first electronic music studios and travelled across Europe to meet other pioneers. He was one of the first British composers to work with musique concrète.

Together with Peter Zinovieff and David Cockerell he founded Electronic Music Studios in London. The company made the first commercially available portable synthesizer, the EMS VCS 3, and later the Synthi 100. Cary also designed the outward appearance of the VCS 3. In 1967 he founded the Royal College of Music's first electronic music studio. In 1974 he moved to the University of Adelaide in Australia, where he taught until 1986 and also wrote as a music critic for The Australian.

He wrote concert works, such as Continuum for band from 1969 and Peccata Mundi from 1972, but was best known for his film and television music. He composed for Doctor Who, including the first story featuring the Daleks, and for the Ealing comedy The Ladykillers from 1955. He also wrote music for the Hammer films Quatermass and the Pit and Blood from the Mummy's Tomb. He died in Adelaide in 2008.
artiest/tristram-cary.listen: Listen to the music of the Daleks in Doctor Who and notice how electronic sounds, without any conventional instruments, create an otherworldly atmosphere.

artiest/trugoy.text:
Trugoy, in full Trugoy the Dove, was the stage name of David Jolicoeur, an American rapper best known as one third of the hip hop group De La Soul. He was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1968, to Haitian-American parents, and grew up in East Massapequa on Long Island. At secondary school he became friends with Vincent Mason, Kelvin Mercer and Paul Huston. Mason, Mercer and he formed De La Soul, under the names Maseo, Posdnuos and Trugoy. He later explained that the first half of his name is simply the word yogurt spelled backwards. Huston, known as Prince Paul, remained the trio's producer.

The debut album 3 Feet High and Rising matched their quirky clothes and positive message, which led critics to call them the hippies of hip hop. With their second album, De La Soul Is Dead (1991), they pointedly shook off that label. The group was also part of the Native Tongues collective. Jolicoeur co-wrote Feel Good Inc. by Gorillaz, a song featuring De La Soul that won a Grammy in 2006 for best pop collaboration with vocals.

In his last years he suffered from heart failure and wore a portable defibrillator, which meant he could not always perform. He died on 12 February 2023, aged 54.
artiest/trugoy.listen: Listen to Buddy by De La Soul and notice how playful and funny the rapping sounds. Which sounds in the background create that effect?

artiest/trys-keturiose.text:
Trys Keturiose is a Lithuanian women's trio that sings sutartinės, an ancient singing tradition from Lithuania. The album Bitela was released in 2017. The group does not sing in the village but as a modern ensemble that brings the tradition back to life.

Sutartinės are polyphonic songs with an open, clear style of singing. The voices sound sharp and bright and move close against one another. This way of singing belongs to the rural tradition of Central and Eastern Europe, where loud singing outdoors, during work and at rituals played a major role. Trys Keturiose is mentioned in the literature as one of the best-known contemporary groups continuing this style.

For pop history, a group like this matters because it shows that singing of a very different kind from Western pop singing is still alive. Such voices and harmonies are a source of inspiration for musicians who look to folk music for something new.
artiest/trys-keturiose.listen: Listen to Bitełė siaubia in balta dobila and notice how the voices wind around one another. Do you hear a lead melody, or do all the voices carry equal weight as they interweave?

artiest/tsuyoshi-yamamoto.text:
Tsuyoshi Yamamoto is a Japanese jazz pianist and composer, born in 1948. He was largely self-taught, although he did have piano lessons as a child. He studied at Nihon University and was already playing professionally while a student. At first he accompanied the pop singer Micky Curtis, with whom he toured Europe in 1967.

In 1974 he became house pianist at Misty, a jazz club in Tokyo. That same year he made his first record as a leader. In the late 1970s he played at major international festivals. For a year he lived in New York, where he performed with, among others, Dizzy Gillespie, Carmen McRae, Sam Jones, Billy Higgins, Elvin Jones and Sonny Stitt. Between 1974 and 2015 he played on sixty-six recording sessions.

Of his 2008 album What a Wonderful Trio!, one reviewer noted that he likes to seek out the very highest regions of the keyboard, with great pleasure. Later he also recorded Life (1976), Star Dust (1997), Autumn in Seattle (2001) and Night at Body and Soul (2015), among others.
artiest/tsuyoshi-yamamoto.listen: Listen to a track from What a Wonderful Trio! and notice how often the piano plays in the high register. What are the bass and drums doing underneath?

artiest/tsuyoshi-yamamoto-trio.text:
The Tsuyoshi Yamamoto Trio centres on the Japanese jazz pianist Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, born in 1948. He was largely self-taught, although he did have piano lessons as a child. As a student at Nihon University he was already playing professionally, at first as an accompanist to the pop singer Micky Curtis, with whom he toured Europe in 1967. In 1974 he became house pianist at Misty, a jazz club in Tokyo. That year he also made his first record as a bandleader. Later he lived in New York for a year, where he played with, among others, Dizzy Gillespie, Carmen McRae, Elvin Jones and Sonny Stitt.

His debut Midnight Sugar was released in 1974, followed by Misty in the same year and Summertime in 1976. In the late 1970s he played at major international festivals. He continued to make records well into the twenty-first century, including What a Wonderful Trio! in 2009. One reviewer remarked that he likes to seek out the highest regions of the keyboard, with great pleasure.

In the history of jazz worldwide, Yamamoto is an example of the flourishing Japanese jazz scene, where piano trios built up a warm, song-oriented tradition of their own.
artiest/tsuyoshi-yamamoto-trio.listen: Listen to Misty and notice how the pianist lets the familiar melody sing freely, with bass and drums as quiet accompanists. Can you hear where he lets go of the melody and where he picks it up again?

artiest/tubeway-army.text:
Tubeway Army was a new wave band from London, formed in 1977 at the height of punk. Singer Gary Webb, who later called himself Gary Numan, was still playing in another group in 1976 and then found the bassist Paul Gardiner. With his uncle Jess Lidyard on drums, the group became a reality. The band signed to the independent label Beggars Banquet and in 1978 released the punk-style single That's Too Bad, which achieved little. After a violent concert in July 1978, Webb decided to turn the group into a studio band.

On the album Tubeway Army from 1978 he used a Minimoog for the first time, almost by accident. The lyrics had dark, science-fiction themes, inspired by writers such as J. G. Ballard and Philip K. Dick. On Replicas in 1979 the synthesizer took the lead. The single Are 'Friends' Electric? and the album both reached number one in England in the summer of 1979. It was the first hit of the electronic age to be built on a synthesizer.

Afterwards Numan dropped the group name and continued under his own name, with the Tubeway Army musicians as his backing band. The band existed only briefly, but it showed that a pop song with a cool, mechanical sound could reach a large audience. In doing so it opened the door to the synth-pop with which the 1980s began. In School of Rock, Are 'Friends' Electric? appears as a listening tip at the start of that era.
artiest/tubeway-army.listen: Listen to Are 'Friends' Electric? and notice the synthesizer that carries both the melody and the bass line. Can you hear how distant and robotic the vocals sound alongside it?

artiest/tubeway-army-gary-numan.text:
Tubeway Army was the British band of singer and musician Gary Numan, born Gary Webb in 1958. The group's first record appeared in 1978 and was not a success at first. After that Numan worked more and more with synthesizers, and it paid off. In 1979 both the single Are “Friends” Electric? and the second album, Replicas, reached number 1 in England.

Shortly afterwards Numan decided to continue under his own name. Later in 1979 the single Cars was released, and that, too, and the album The Pleasure Principle reached number 1. In 1980 a third album, Telekon, followed at number one. He had hits until the middle of the 1980s, after which his popularity declined. He kept making records and performing, however, and in the 2010s appreciation grew again: Savage (Songs from a Broken World) from 2017 reached number two.

With Tubeway Army and his first solo records, Numan became one of the pioneers of British electronic pop music. His music sounded cool and mechanical, with heavy synthesizer sounds and a distant, almost robotic vocal style, and lyrics about alienation and machines. In this way he brought the synthesizer to the top of the British charts in 1979.
artiest/tubeway-army-gary-numan.listen: Listen to Are “Friends” Electric? and notice the heavy, slow synthesizer part that carries the song. Hear how Numan speaks more than he sings, in a flat, detached voice.

artiest/tupac-shakur.text:
Tupac Amaru Shakur, also known as 2Pac and Makaveli, was an American rapper and actor. He was born in East Harlem, New York, in 1971, the son of members of the Black Panther Party. His name referred to Túpac Amaru II, a descendant of the last Inca ruler, who was executed in 1781. His mother, Afeni Shakur, raised him alone. In 1984 the family moved to Baltimore, where he studied acting, poetry, jazz and ballet at the Baltimore School for the Arts. In 1988 he went to the San Francisco Bay Area.

His debut album 2Pacalypse Now (1991) made him, with its political raps, a central figure in West Coast hip hop. Me Against the World (1995) and All Eyez on Me (1996) followed, the latter the first double album in hip hop, with the hits California Love and How Do U Want It. He formed the group Thug Life and worked with Snoop Dogg, Dr. Dre and the Outlawz. He also acted in films such as Juice, Poetic Justice and Above the Rim. In November 1994 he was shot five times in a studio in New York, and later he spent eight months in prison. After that he signed to Death Row Records and became caught up in the rivalry between the East and West Coasts. On 7 September 1996 he was shot near Paradise, Nevada, and he died six days later.

His lyrics dealt partly with social injustice and the position of African Americans, and partly they were gangsta rap. In 2017 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/tupac-shakur.listen: Listen to California Love and compare it with a track from Me Against the World. What changes in the tone of the voice and the lyrics?

artiest/turlough-o-carolan.text:
Turlough O'Carolan was a blind Irish harper, composer and singer, born in 1670 in Nobber, County Meath, the son of a blacksmith. During the civil wars his family lost its estates and moved in 1684 to County Roscommon, where the MacDermot Roe family took them in. Mrs MacDermot Roe saw to his education. At eighteen he lost his sight to smallpox. She then had him apprenticed to a good harper. At twenty-one he was given a horse and a guide and set out across Ireland to write songs for patrons.

For almost fifty years he travelled from one end of the country to the other, composing and playing his melodies. He often wrote the melody first, on horseback along the way, and added the words later. Many pieces are called planxty, a word he probably coined or popularised for a tribute to a generous host. Usually he dedicated a song to a particular patron, and in return he was received as an honoured guest. Because he did not speak much English, he wrote only one song in English, Carolan's Devotion. About a third of his surviving music has Irish words.

His music shows the influence of the classical music of the Continent, while pieces such as Farewell to Music reveal a much older, Gaelic harp style. Some therefore call him the national composer of Ireland. Modern musicians have often adapted his repertoire to the jigs and reels of today. He died in 1738.
artiest/turlough-o-carolan.listen: Listen to a melody by O'Carolan, such as Farewell to Music, on harp and notice the songlike line. Does this sound more like Irish folk music or like Baroque music?

artiest/turnstile.text:
Turnstile is an American rock band from Baltimore, Maryland, formed in 2010. The group emerged from the city's hardcore scene and consists of singer Brendan Yates, guitarists Pat McCrory and Meg Mills, bassist Franz Lyons and drummer Daniel Fang. After two EPs, Pressure to Succeed in 2011 and Step 2 Rhythm in 2013, the debut album Nonstop Feeling was released in 2015. In 2018 came Time & Space, their first album on a major label.

The breakthrough came in 2021 with Glow On. The album was highly praised by critics, received three Grammy nominations and ranked high in Rolling Stone's end-of-year lists. The fourth album, Never Enough from 2025, reached the top ten in five countries, including the United States. With it the band won the Grammy for best rock album in 2026, and with the song Birds the one for best metal performance.

Turnstile began as a hardcore band but looked for more melody and colour than the genre usually allows. The sound remains hard and fast, with heavy guitars and a tight rhythm section, but there is room for vocals that stick in the mind. In this way the band fits into School of Rock's story of rock becoming popular again: while Måneskin won the Eurovision Song Contest and Olivia Rodrigo brought pop-punk to the charts, a hardcore band was also filling large venues again.
artiest/turnstile.listen: Listen to Birds by Turnstile. Notice how the hard guitars and the fast tempo go together with a vocal melody that is easy to sing along to.

artiest/twarres.text:
Twarres is a folk and pop band from Warga in Friesland that sings in both English and Frisian. The name comes from the Frisian word twaresom, which means the two of them. At the beginning the core of the group was the duo Mirjam Timmer and Johan van der Veen. With Wêr bisto the pair won the audience prize at the Frisian song festival Liet in 1999. The song was re-recorded at EMI after Paul de Leeuw invited the duo onto his programme, and in 2000 it became a huge hit in the Netherlands and Flanders, the first Frisian-language number one in the Netherlands. Marco Borsato asked them to join him on stage during his concerts.

The singles She Couldn't Laugh, Children and I Need To Know followed, and the debut album Stream (2001) went platinum. In 2002 Twarres received an Edison for best new group. The second album was called CD². The sound is rich and harmonious, with vocals at the centre and acoustic instruments such as piano and violin. At the end of 2003 the group gave its last concert, in the old dairy factory in Warga where it all began.

The band later returned, but Van der Veen left in 2007 for health reasons. Timmer started a solo career as Mir in 2006. In 2017 Twarres consisted of Timmer and the brothers Julian and Kristian Dijkstra, who recorded the single Fûgelfrij. Twarres showed that a Frisian title and lyrics could reach a large audience.
artiest/twarres.listen: Listen to Wêr bisto and notice the sound of Frisian in a pop song. Can you hear where the piano and the violin carry the melody?

artiest/twisted-sister.text:
Twisted Sister is an American heavy metal band, formed in 1972 in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey, and later based on Long Island. The group grew out of Silver Star, a glitter band that wanted to be the New York version of the New York Dolls. The name Twisted Sister came from singer Michael O'Neill in 1973. In its early years the band played almost every night, and by 1974 guitarist Jay Jay French had already clocked up nearly six hundred nights. In 1982 the line-up that recorded the first four albums came together: Jay Jay French and Eddie Ojeda on guitar, Dee Snider as singer, Mark Mendoza on bass and A. J. Pero on drums.

The first albums, Under the Blade (1982) and You Can't Stop Rock 'n' Roll (1983), were well received and made the band known in the underground. The breakthrough came with Stay Hungry (1984) and the single We're Not Gonna Take It, their only song in the top 40 of the American Hot 100. Come Out and Play (1985) and Love Is for Suckers (1987) did less well, and in 1988 the group broke up. In 2003 it returned for good, with Still Hungry (2004) and A Twisted Christmas (2006). After Pero's death in 2015 a farewell tour followed.

The group is as well known for its hairstyles and androgynous clothing and make-up as for its music, and is counted among the hair metal of the 1980s. Its music videos for We're Not Gonna Take It and I Wanna Rock stood out for their slapstick. In this way the band showed that hard rock was allowed to be funny.
artiest/twisted-sister.listen: Listen to We're Not Gonna Take It and notice the chorus sung along by a crowd. Why does this chorus suit a stadium full of people?

artiest/two-steps-from-hell.text:
Two Steps from Hell was an American music production company based in Los Angeles. It was founded in 2006 by the composers Thomas Bergersen and Nick Phoenix, a Norwegian and an Englishman. They began with demos for film trailers, which were distributed and licensed exclusively within the film advertising world. They wrote separately from each other but released their work together. Over time they supplied music for thousands of trailers and TV commercials, including for the Harry Potter, Pirates of the Caribbean, Star Trek and Twilight film series.

When the public heard the music, fans online asked to be able to buy the tracks. In 2010 the first albums appeared, Invincible and Archangel, with their most popular demos. In 2012 came SkyWorld, consisting of entirely new music. In 2013 they gave their first concert, in the Walt Disney Concert Hall. Later, thirteen releases reached the top ten of the Billboard Classical Crossover chart, three of them at number one: Battlecry, Unleashed and Myth. In 2024 Bergersen and Phoenix parted ways.

The music is orchestral and choral, with modern additions, and structured like a pop song. Its powerful, solemn tone gave rise to the term epic music. Pieces such as Heart of Courage from 2010 and Protectors of the Earth from 2010 show how film music can take on a life of its own outside the film, as music that people seek out and listen to for themselves.
artiest/two-steps-from-hell.listen: Listen to Heart of Courage. Notice how the piece begins softly and slowly grows to a grand finale with choir and orchestra, as if it were a short film scene without images.

artiest/two-steps-from-hell-thomas-berge.text: Two Steps from Hell was founded in Los Angeles in 2006 by the Norwegian Thomas Bergersen and the Englishman Nick Phoenix. It was not a band but a production company for trailer music: short, powerful pieces that film studios licensed for their trailers, including for Harry Potter, Star Trek and Pirates of the Caribbean. At first this music was intended only for the film industry. Because of public demand, the first public album, Invincible, with Heart of Courage, was released in 2010. Archangel followed in 2011. Their style, called epic music, consists of choir, big percussion, ostinatos in the strings and a climax that arrives quickly.
artiest/two-steps-from-hell-thomas-berge.listen: Listen to the build-up in blocks: a quiet opening, a rhythmic string ostinato, then choir and heavy drums heading for an early climax.

artiest/tyagaraja.text: Tyagaraja was a composer and singer from Tamil Nadu who devoted his life to the worship of the god Rama. About 720 of his kritis survive, songs mostly in Telugu in which text, raga and rhythm together form a prayer. His five Pancharatna kritis are sung together by musicians every year in Thiruvaiyaru, where he is buried. Almost every Carnatic concert still includes a song by him.
artiest/tyagaraja.listen: Listen to Jagadanandakaraka, the first Pancharatna kriti, sung by M. Balamuralikrishna: hear how the singer repeats a line and adds something to it with each repetition.

artiest/tyla.text:
Tyla Seethal was born in 2002 in Edenvale, near Johannesburg, and grew up in the South African city. During her final school year she posted her own songs and covers on Instagram and spent every weekend in the studio. In 2019 her first single, Getting Late, was released and was a success in her home country. In 2021 she signed to Epic Records, while she was actually studying mining engineering. Her parents gave her a year off to try her luck.

The international breakthrough song was Water in 2023. A dance challenge on TikTok made it known worldwide. Tyla was the first South African solo artist in 55 years in the American Billboard Hot 100, after Hugh Masekela with Grazing in the Grass in 1968. In 2024 she won the first Grammy for Best African Music Performance with Water. Her self-titled debut album Tyla came out in March 2024, and the second album, A*Pop, followed in 2026.

She calls her style Popiano: a blend of pop and amapiano, the South African house style with slow, rolling rhythms and deep bass lines. Tyla shows that today's African dance music can break straight into the global pop charts, without first having to resemble a Western sound.
artiest/tyla.listen: Listen to Water and notice the rhythmic foundation beneath her vocals. Can you hear how the beat stays relaxed and danceable while the singing glides loosely over it?

artiest/typhoon.text:
Typhoon is the stage name of rapper and singer Glenn de Randamie, born in 1984 in 't Harde on the Veluwe, into a musical family of Surinamese descent. His father played guitar and saxophone, his mother sang in a choir, and his brother raps as Blaxtar. At fifteen he started in the group Rudeteenz, together with a member of the Zwolle rap group Opgezwolle and his brother. He completed his pre-university secondary education (vwo) in Zwolle and in 2004 won the Grote Prijs van Nederland. After that he signed to the hip hop label Top Notch.

In 2007 his debut Tussen licht en lucht was released, with influences from hip hop, jazz and African and Eastern music. He formed the group Fakkelbrigade, made the EP Chocolade with New Cool Collective and in 2009 received the Zilveren Harp. After that things went quiet for a while: Typhoon was overworked and was searching for his own musical identity. In 2014 Lobi da Basi was released, Surinamese for love rules. The album was also well received outside hip hop, OOR placed it second among the best albums of that year, and the single Hemel valt became popular in the Netherlands and Suriname. In 2020 Lichthuis followed.

Typhoon raps in Dutch, in a personal and reflective way, about faith, love, identity and origins. His music blends hip hop with jazz and other styles, and he often played with a live band, such as New Cool Collective. In this way he belongs to the Zwolle hip hop scene around Opgezwolle, and showed that Dutch-language rap could also reach the large pop festival audience.
artiest/typhoon.listen: Listen to Hemel valt and notice how Typhoon distributes his words over the beat: which phrases get emphasis, and where does he leave space? Also listen for which instruments you recognise alongside the beat.

artiest/u-roy.text:
U-Roy, born Ewart Beckford, was a Jamaican singer and a pioneer of toasting, the rhythmic talking or singing over an instrumental recording. He was born in 1942 in Jones Town, Kingston, into a religious and musical family. His nickname came from a young relative who could not pronounce his first name. As a boy he listened to Louis Prima, James Brown and Fats Domino, and he was influenced above all by Louis Jordan's phrasing. In 1961 he began as a deejay with various sound systems, including that of Sir Coxsone Dodd, and later at King Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi.

In 1969 he toasted there over instrumental dubplates made from existing rocksteady recordings. His first single was Dynamic Fashion Way, followed by Earth's Rightful Ruler with Peter Tosh. After a tip from John Holt he ended up with producer Duke Reid. In 1970 Wake the Town, Rule the Nation and Wear You to the Ball occupied the top three places on both Jamaican charts at the same time. As a result, deejaying, which had previously belonged mainly to live performances, also became a successful form on record. In 1971 his version of The Paragons' The Tide Is High was released.

In 1972 he toured England for the first time. The album Dread in a Babylon (1975) was released on Virgin Records and sold well in the United Kingdom. Natty Rebel (1976), Rasta Ambassador (1977) and Jah Son Of Africa (1978) followed. In 1978 he started his own sound system, Stur Gav, which launched a younger generation of toasters. He died in 2021.
artiest/u-roy.listen: Listen to Wake the Town and notice how U-Roy lays his voice over the rhythm section like a second instrument. Where exactly does he sit in the rhythm?

artiest/u-s-a-for-africa.text:
U.S.A. for Africa was a group of American artists who in 1985 recorded the charity single We Are the World. The occasion was Do They Know It's Christmas? by the British Band Aid from 1984. Harry Belafonte decided to make an American counterpart to raise money for the famine in Ethiopia, which between 1983 and 1985 cost about a million people their lives. Manager Ken Kragen brought in his clients Lionel Richie and Kenny Rogers, and they asked Stevie Wonder. Quincy Jones became producer and called Michael Jackson, who had just finished the Victory Tour with The Jacksons.

Jackson and Richie wrote the song together at the Jackson family home in Encino, California. They wanted a song that was easy to sing, easy to remember and hymn-like. Recording began at Kenny Rogers' Lion Share Recording Studio in Los Angeles. First session musicians such as drummer John Robinson, bassist Louis Johnson and pianist Greg Phillinganes recorded the backing, and then the singers followed. Among them were Bruce Springsteen, Cyndi Lauper, Paul Simon, Stevie Wonder and Tina Turner. The line about taking one's own life was changed, because it could be read as a reference to suicide.

Columbia Records released the song on 7 March 1985. It topped the charts in many countries, won four Grammys and raised more than 80 million dollars for aid in Africa and the United States. In 2010 a new version followed after the earthquake in Haiti.
artiest/u-s-a-for-africa.listen: Listen to We Are the World and notice how the voices of famous singers alternate and come together in the chorus. How many voices do you recognise?

artiest/u-srinivas.text:
Uppalapu Srinivas was born in 1969 in Palakollu in Andhra Pradesh and died in 2014. At the age of five he picked up his father's mandolin. His father, who had studied classical music, bought a new instrument and taught him to play. Later he was taught by the singer Rudraraju Subbaraju, who sang pieces from the Carnatic repertoire, after which the six-year-old Srinivas played them back on the mandolin. In this way he developed a style of his own on an instrument that had never been played in such a strict Carnatic manner. He gave his first concert in Chennai at the age of eleven, in 1981.

Srinivas was the first to use the electric mandolin in Carnatic music. He adapted the instrument with five single strings instead of four double ones, so that it suited the pitch, the raga system and the gamakas, the fine, ornamental oscillations in pitch. At the age of thirteen he played at the Berlin Jazz Festival, where he received a standing ovation. He worked with John McLaughlin, Michael Brook and Zakir Hussain and played in Remember Shakti.

He recorded more than 137 albums, from Carnatic solo programmes to fusion and world music. For many listeners outside India, his playing was their first introduction to South Indian classical music.
artiest/u-srinivas.listen: Listen to Samajavaragamana and notice how the mandolin sustains long, singing notes. Try to hear how he embellishes the melody with small gliding movements, as a singer would.

artiest/u2.text:
U2 is an Irish rock band from Dublin. In 1976 the fourteen-year-old drummer Larry Mullen Jr. put a note on the notice board of his school, Mount Temple. Those who responded included Paul Hewson, known as Bono, the guitarist who calls himself The Edge, and Adam Clayton. They could barely play, but punk had taught them that being able to play was no prerequisite. Within four years they signed to Island Records and the debut album Boy was released in 1980.

With War in 1983 the band broke through in the United Kingdom. Sunday Bloody Sunday and Pride (In the Name of Love) made U2 known as a politically and socially engaged group. On The Unforgettable Fire in 1984 the group worked with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois for the first time, which brought a more ambient sound. After the performance at Live Aid in 1985 came The Joshua Tree in 1987, the album that made them world famous. In the 1990s the band reinvented itself with Achtung Baby and the Zoo TV Tour, with influences from alternative rock, industrial and electronic dance music.

The sound revolves around Bono's vocals and The Edge's echoing, effects-laden guitar playing. It is big, anthemic and suited to stadiums. Bono, the band and their performances also remained active outside music for human rights and good causes.
artiest/u2.listen: Listen to Sunday Bloody Sunday and notice the drums at the start: they sound like a military march. Can you hear how the guitar sound builds tension before Bono begins to sing?

artiest/uan-rasey.text:
Uan Rasey was an American trumpeter, best known for his studio work. He was born in 1921 in Glasgow, Montana, and taught himself to play the trumpet as a child. In 1937 he moved with his family to Los Angeles, where he began playing professionally with bandleaders such as Sonny Dunham, Ozzie Nelson and Alvino Rey. As a child he contracted polio, and throughout his career he played the trumpet on crutches. He was a keen follower of athletics and wanted a contract at MGM stating that he did not have to work on Saturdays, the day of the matches.

From 1949 until the early 1970s he was first choice on trumpet at MGM and other studio orchestras. He played on a great deal of film music, including An American in Paris, Singin' in the Rain, Gigi, Ben-Hur, West Side Story, My Fair Lady and Spartacus. His trumpet solo in Chinatown, Jerry Goldsmith's Oscar-nominated score from 1974, is well known. In All the Fine Young Cannibals he played the music for Robert Wagner's character. He also played on records by Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole, Mel Tormé, Doris Day, Judy Garland and The Monkees.

He taught until a great age, his pupils including Arturo Sandoval and Jack Sheldon. In 2009 he received the Honorary Award of the International Trumpet Guild, its highest distinction. He died in 2011. Rasey shows how much Hollywood owed to musicians you never saw on a poster.
artiest/uan-rasey.listen: Listen to the trumpet solo in the film music of Chinatown and notice the soft, lonely sound. What mood does the trumpet evoke?

artiest/udo-jurgens.text:
Udo Jürgens was born Jürgen Udo Bockelmann in 1934 and grew into one of the best-known Austrian composers and singers in the German-speaking world. As early as 1952 he was playing with his own quartet in Klagenfurt, in dance and jazz cafés. He wrote nearly a thousand songs and performed to packed halls in Germany, Austria and Switzerland until his death in 2014.

After two earlier attempts, he won the Eurovision Song Contest for Austria in 1966 with Merci, Chérie. His song Warum nur, warum? from 1964 was recorded by Matt Monro as Walk Away and reached the top of the British charts. Later came Griechischer Wein, Aber bitte mit Sahne and Mit 66 Jahren. He sang Buenos Días, Argentina in 1978 together with the German national football team. In 1979 his disco record Udo '80 was released. His songs inspired the musical Ich war noch niemals in New York in 2007.

Jürgens broadened German-language pop beyond the traditional post-war schlager repertoire. He combined it with a modern pop sound and with French chanson, and his melodies reached listeners of all ages. Since 2015 he has been recorded as the artist who has spent the longest time in the charts, well over fifty-seven years.
artiest/udo-jurgens.listen: Listen to Griechischer Wein and notice the difference between the calm verse and the singalong chorus. Where do you hear the wistfulness in the melody?

artiest/ultravox.text:
Ultravox was a British new wave band, formed in London in April 1974 under the name Tiger Lily. The driving force at first was singer and lyricist Dennis Leigh, who came to call himself John Foxx. He played with drummer Warren Cann and violinist Billy Currie. In 1976 the group signed to Island Records and came up with the name Ultravox!, the exclamation mark being a reference to the krautrock band Neu!. The band drew inspiration from Roxy Music, David Bowie and Kraftwerk. The first records from 1977, Ultravox!, Ha! Ha! Ha! and then Systems of Romance in 1978, sold modestly.

In 1979 Foxx left for a solo career. Midge Ure took over as singer and guitarist, after working with Currie on the studio project Visage. With him the group achieved the success that had previously eluded it. Between 1980 and 1986 Ultravox had seven albums in the British top ten and seventeen singles in the top forty. The best-known song is Vienna from 1981, from the album of the same name. Rage in Eden, Quartet and Lament, among others, followed. In 1987 the group split up.

Ultravox brought the cool electronics of the synthesizer together with strings and dramatic vocals. Ure also remained active as a writer and producer. His greatest moment came in 1984, when, together with a colleague, he wrote Do They Know It's Christmas?, the charity record that characterises the 1980s. In 2008 the best-known line-up came together once more and made the album Brill!ant in 2012.
artiest/ultravox.listen: Listen to Vienna by Ultravox. Notice the piano, the violin and the synthesizer that slowly build the song towards a grand chorus.

artiest/uncle-dave-macon.text:
David Harrison Macon, better known as Uncle Dave Macon, was born in Tennessee in 1870. At fifteen he learned to play the banjo from a circus comedian. In his youth his family ran a hotel in Nashville, where travelling performers stayed, and later he hauled freight with mules and entertained people along the way with singing and banjo playing. He did not become a professional musician until around the age of fifty. As a vaudeville performer he appeared in the Loew's theatres, and in 1924 he made his first recordings, for Vocalion in New York, with fiddler Sid Harkreader.

In 1925 Macon became one of the first performers on the radio station WSM in Nashville. He is considered the first star of the Grand Ole Opry. With guitarist Sam McGee he formed a regular duo, and in 1927 he started the Fruit Jar Drinkers. His repertoire consisted of traditional songs, jokes and new pieces, delivered with a generous dose of showmanship. His distinctive appearance, with hat, gold teeth and high collar, made him recognisable. He performed until shortly before his death in 1952.

Macon is seen as the bridge between nineteenth-century folk music and vaudeville on the one hand and the gramophone and radio of the twentieth century on the other. The historian Charles Wolfe called him the grandfather of country music.
artiest/uncle-dave-macon.listen: Listen to Keep My Skillet Good and Greasy and notice the lively banjo and the playful way of singing. Can you hear that it is almost a stage number, with humour and a cheerful energy?

artiest/uncle-waffles.text:
Uncle Waffles is the stage name of Lungelihle Zwane, a DJ and producer from Eswatini who works in South Africa. She was born in 2000, grew up with her grandmother and listened to South African house and kwaito by, among others, Black Coffee and Lebo Mathosa. At first she presented on Swazi television, where she came into contact with DJ equipment. Then she moved to South Africa to study. During the coronavirus lockdowns in 2020 she learned to DJ and, by her own account, practised eight hours a day.

Her breakthrough came in October 2021, when she stepped in at a club in Soweto. A video of her dancing during her set to Adiwele by Young Stunna went viral. She specialises in amapiano, a South African style, and Billboard called her the Princess of Amapiano. Her debut single Tanzania was released in March 2022, together with the EP Red Dragon, and went to number one in South Africa. Rolling Stone placed the song at number eight on its list of the best Afropop songs of that year. The EPs Asylum and Solace (2023) followed later. In 2022 she toured the United Kingdom and Ireland, and was given a residency at BBC Radio 1.

In April 2023 she was the first amapiano musician at the Coachella festival. Beyoncé used a sample of Tanzania in a dance break during her Renaissance World Tour. Uncle Waffles shows how an African dance style could reach a worldwide audience through social media.
artiest/uncle-waffles.listen: Listen to Tanzania and notice the rhythmic foundation and the repetition that gets you dancing straight away. Which sounds stay with you?

artiest/uncle-waffles-en-tony-duardo.text:
Uncle Waffles is the stage name of Lungelihle Zwane, a DJ and producer from Eswatini who works in South Africa. She was born in 2000 and was at first a television presenter. In 2020 she learned to DJ during the lockdowns and, by her own account, practised eight hours a day. In October 2021 she stepped in for a DJ at a club in Soweto and a video of her dancing during her set went viral.

Her first single, Tanzania, was released in March 2022, shortly before the EP Red Dragon. The song reached number one in South Africa. Rolling Stone named it one of the best Afropop songs of 2022. The EPs Asylum and Solace followed in 2023, with Echoes, on which the producer Tony Duardo takes part. In April 2023 she was the first amapiano artist at Coachella. Beyoncé used Tanzania in a dance moment on her Renaissance World Tour.

Amapiano is a South African dance style with rolling bass, slow house beats and jazzy piano sounds. Uncle Waffles brought that sound to festivals and radio far beyond Africa, thanks in part to her dancing and her presence on social media. Tanzania is the best-known example.
artiest/uncle-waffles-en-tony-duardo.listen: Listen to Tanzania and notice how little happens: a calm, deep bass line and a light rhythm that slowly builds. Can you hear how the groove sets you swaying without any effort?

artiest/united-states-marine-band-john-p.text:
The United States Marine Band is the military band of the United States Marine Corps, known as The President's Own. It achieved its greatest fame under John Philip Sousa, born in 1854 in Washington. His father, a trombonist in the band, enrolled him as an apprentice at the age of thirteen, to prevent him from joining a circus band. Sousa left the band in 1875, played violin in a theatre orchestra and learned to conduct. In 1880 he returned as its leader and stayed for twelve years.

Under Sousa the Marine Band became the best military band in the country. He shifted the repertoire towards symphonic music and insisted on stricter rehearsals. He led the band under five presidents. In 1892 he started his own civilian Sousa Band, which until 1931 gave more than fifteen thousand concerts in the United States and abroad, including at the world exhibition in Paris and at the Royal Albert Hall in London. Sousa also helped develop the sousaphone, a marching tuba.

His marches made him known as the March King. The Stars and Stripes Forever is the national march of the United States. Other well-known pieces are Semper Fidelis, The Liberty Bell and The Washington Post. His marches are still the sound of parades, football stadiums and holidays.
artiest/united-states-marine-band-john-p.listen: Listen to The Stars and Stripes Forever and notice the piccolo, which sings out above the brass in the final section. Can you hear how the march is built in blocks and becomes more and more cheerful?

artiest/urbanator.text:
Urbanator is a jazz project of the Polish musician Michał Urbaniak, who played violin, lyricon and saxophone. Urbaniak was born in 1943 in Warsaw and in the 1960s played with, among others, Andrzej Trzaskowski and the quintet of Krzysztof Komeda. He performed at the Montreux festival, where in 1971 he won the Grand Prix for best soloist. In 1973 he emigrated with the singer Urszula Dudziak to the United States, where he signed to Columbia Records and with his band Fusion combined Polish folk music with funky jazz from New York.

Innovative projects followed later. Urbanator is described as the first band to mix rap and hip hop with jazz. He also released Urbanizer, a project with a four-man R&B vocal group from 1978, and UrbSymphony. In 1995 UrbSymphony performed with a rapper and a symphony orchestra of sixty musicians, and that concert was recorded. The albums by Urbanator are Urbanator II (1996) and Urbanator (2022).

From 1970 Urbaniak played a five-string violin made especially for him, a violin synthesizer nicknamed the talking violin, alongside soprano, alto and tenor saxophone and lyricon, an electronic wind instrument that resembles a saxophone. He played with, among others, Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea, Wayne Shorter and Joe Zawinul, and in 1985 Miles Davis invited him to the recording sessions for Tutu. He died in 2025. Urbanator shows that the boundary between jazz and hip hop was crossed early on.
artiest/urbanator.listen: Listen to a track from Urbanator II and notice how a rapper and a jazz band alternate. Which instruments set the rhythm?

artiest/urszula-dudziak.text: Urszula Dudziak was born in 1943 in Straconka, in the south of Poland. She began as a singer of jazz standards and from the 1960s sang in the group of the violinist Michał Urbaniak, whom she married. She developed a style of her own, often without words: she uses her voice as an instrument, with high flourishes, rhythmic sounds and electronic effects such as echo. In 1973 she moved to New York with Urbaniak. Papaya (1975) became her best-known song. Later she sang with Gil Evans's orchestra and with the Vienna Art Orchestra. She is one of the best-known jazz singers in Poland.
artiest/urszula-dudziak.listen: Hear how the voice sings no words, but sounds like an instrument with effects.

artiest/us3.text:
Us3 is a British jazz rap group, founded in 1992 by the London producer Geoff Wilkinson. The name comes from Us Three, a 1960 album by Horace Parlan, produced by Alfred Lion, the founder of Blue Note Records. The debut album Hand on the Torch used samples of Blue Note tracks from Lion's catalogue. Jazz rap is a hip hop genre that uses jazz recordings as its basis.

In the early 1990s Wilkinson made two recordings under the name Us3. In 1990 Where Will We Be in the 21st Century was released, a limited-edition white-label record that attracted the attention of the independent label Ninja Tune. In 1991 came the single The Band Played The Boogie by NW1, with the British rapper Born 2 B. After that he founded Us3 with his production partner Mel Simpson. One of their demos, recorded in March 1992, was Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia), featuring the British trumpeter Gerard Presencer. The song uses a sample of Cantaloupe Island by Herbie Hancock. In 1993 it became world famous and in the Netherlands was made an Alarmschijf (Dutch national radio's "alarm record" for a rising hit), after which it reached number eighteen in the Top 40.

Albums followed such as Broadway & 52nd in 1996, An Ordinary Day in an Unusual Place in 2001 and Schizophonic in 2006. In 2014 the group laid down its work. Wilkinson turned to film and library music. In 2025 Soundtrack was released, with trap rhythms and big band orchestration. Us3 showed that jazz and hip hop reinforce each other well.
artiest/us3.listen: Listen to Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia). Notice the recognisable piano loop from Cantaloupe Island, the trumpet and the calm hip hop rhythm underneath.

artiest/usha-iyer.text:
Usha Iyer, better known as Usha Uthup, is an Indian singer with a deep contralto voice who sings in many genres and languages. She was born in 1947 in Mumbai into a Tamil family. At school she was thrown out of music class because her voice did not fit in, but her teacher saw that she was musical and gave her castanets and a triangle. At home she heard Western classical music, Hindustani and Carnatic music, and listened to Radio Ceylon. At the age of nine she sang in public for the first time, on Radio Ceylon's Ovaltine Music Hour.

In 1969 she began her career in a nightclub in Chennai. After that she sang in clubs in Calcutta, Mumbai and Delhi. In Delhi a film crew working with Dev Anand asked her for playback singing. She made her Bollywood debut with Bombay Talkie (1970) and also sang in Hare Rama Hare Krishna (1971), where she sang a line in English. In 1968 she recorded covers of pop songs, such as Jambalaya and Scotch and Soda, which sold well. In Nairobi she became so popular that President Jomo Kenyatta gave her the honorary title of citizen of Kenya. There she sang Malaika with Fadhili Williams.

In the 1970s and 1980s she sang for composers such as R. D. Burman and Bappi Lahiri and made songs such as Mehbooba Mehbooba and Dum Maro Dum popular in her own way. In this way she built up a kind of Indian pop of her own, a blend of Western and Indian music. In 2011 she received the Padma Shri and in 2024 the Padma Bhushan.
artiest/usha-iyer.listen: Listen to a recording by Usha Uthup and notice the low, powerful voice. What would you hear if the same melody were sung by a high-voiced singer?

artiest/usha-mangeshkar.text:
Usha Mangeshkar is an Indian singer, born in 1935, who has recorded in many languages, including Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Kannada, Nepali, Gujarati, Odia and Assamese. She is the youngest of the four Mangeshkar sisters, after Lata Mangeshkar, Meena Khadikar and Asha Bhosle, and the older sister of Hridaynath Mangeshkar. That family plays a major role in Indian film music.

She came into the spotlight as a playback singer with devotional songs for the 1975 film Jai Santoshi Maa, which became an enormous success. For her song Main to Aarti from that film she was nominated for the Filmfare Award for best female playback singer, and for this film she also won the prize of the Bengal Film Journalists' Association. Later came nominations for Mangta Hai To Aaja from Inkaar (1977) and Humse Nazar To Milao from Ikraar (1980). In 2006 she sang the same songs again for the remake of the film.

She is known for Mungda and for songs for the Marathi film Pinjara. She also sang Chupi Chupi Gori Kane in the Odia film Abhiman (1977) and created the musical drama Phoolwanti for Indian television, Doordarshan. In 2020 she received a Mirchi Award for lifetime achievement and the Lata Mangeshkar Award of the government of Maharashtra. In 2025 the Filmfare Marathi Lifetime Achievement Award followed. Her career shows how broad the field was in which a playback singer could work.
artiest/usha-mangeshkar.listen: Listen to Main to Aarti from Jai Santoshi Maa and notice the devotional tone of the singing. How does a song sound that is meant to be prayed along to?

artiest/usher.text:
Usher Raymond IV was born in 1978 in Dallas, Texas, and grew up in Chattanooga, Tennessee. At the age of nine he sang in the church youth choir. The family then moved to Atlanta, where there were more opportunities for young singers. At twelve he became a member of the R&B group NuBeginning, and in 1994, at fifteen, his first album, Usher, was released. The breakthrough came in 1997 with My Way, on which Nice & Slow became his first number one on the American Hot 100.

The third album, 8701, from 2001 yielded, among others, U Remind Me and U Got It Bad. Confessions from 2004 is the best-selling album by a Black artist in the twenty-first century, with the number one hits Yeah!, Burn, Confessions Part II and My Boo. Later came Here I Stand in 2008, with Love in This Club, and Raymond v. Raymond in 2010, with OMG. With these he topped the American chart in three consecutive decades. Billboard named him the second most successful artist of the 2000s.

Usher is a singer, songwriter, dancer and actor. His music moves from smooth R&B to dance and electronic production, always with a soft, flexible voice. In 2008 he founded the label Raymond-Braun Media Group to guide the career of Justin Bieber, and in 2024 he performed the Super Bowl halftime show. In School of Rock he belongs to the singers who scored hit after hit in the 1990s and 2000s, together with Rihanna.
artiest/usher.listen: Listen to Yeah! by Usher. Notice how short and rhythmic the vocals are and how the beat is given room to carry the song.

artiest/utfo.text:
UTFO, short for Untouchable Force Organization, was an American hip hop group from Brooklyn, New York. The group formed in the early 1980s under the name UFO, but that was already taken by an English rock band, so it became UTFO. The members were Kangol Kid, Educated Rapper, Doctor Ice and Mix Master Ice. Kangol Kid and Doctor Ice had first been a dance duo, the Keystone Dancers, and danced with Whodini. The members of UTFO were the first breakdancers to appear on The Phil Donahue Show.

In 1984 the group signed to Select Records, Fred Munao's label, and released Roxanne, Roxanne, originally the B-side of Hangin' Out. The song hit the hip hop world like a bomb. It led to a record twenty-five answer records in a single year, the Roxanne Wars, and eventually to more than a hundred. The best-known response was that by Roxanne Shanté, which came about around producer Marley Marl, and that was the first rap feud in hip hop. The debut album UTFO (1985) was produced by the R&B group Full Force, who brought in the sampling specialist Gary Pozner. That was one of the first times the E-mu Emulator was heard on a commercial record. Skeezer Pleezer (1986), with Split Personality, Lethal (1987), Doin' It! (1989) and Bag It & Bone It (1991) followed.

In 2008 Roxanne, Roxanne ranked number 84 on VH1's 100 Greatest Songs of Hip Hop. Educated Rapper died in 2017, Kangol Kid in 2021.
artiest/utfo.listen: Listen to Roxanne, Roxanne and notice how the rappers alternate and what role the sample and the drum machine play. Why could so many others make an answer to this?

artiest/valery-gergiev.text:
Valery Gergiev is a Russian conductor and opera director, born in 1953 in Moscow and raised in Vladikavkaz in North Ossetia. From 1972 to 1977 he studied at the Leningrad Conservatoire, with Ilya Musin as his main conducting teacher. In 1978 he became assistant conductor at the Kirov Opera, today's Mariinsky Opera, where he made his debut with Sergei Prokofiev's War and Peace. Since 1988 he has been artistic director of the Mariinsky, and in 1996 he was appointed general director.

In the West he broke through in the 1980s and 1990s. In 1985 he made his British debut, in 1988 he stood before the London Symphony Orchestra for the first time, and in 1991 he conducted Modest Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov in Munich. From 1995 to 2008 he was principal conductor of the Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra. In 2007 he became principal conductor of the London Symphony Orchestra, and in 2015 of the Munich Philharmonic. At the end of 2023 he also became artistic director of the Bolshoi Theatre. He is the first to lead both theatres at the same time, and he also organises the White Nights festival in St Petersburg. At a concert in Palmyra in 2016 and one in Tskhinvali in 2008 he commemorated victims of violence.

Gergiev is controversial because of his support for the Russian regime of Vladimir Putin. In March 2022 Munich dismissed him, because he refused to condemn the Russian invasion of Ukraine. That makes him an example of how politics and classical music can become intertwined.
artiest/valery-gergiev.listen: Listen to a recording of Gergiev with the London Symphony Orchestra, for example a symphony by Prokofiev, and notice how the orchestra grows from very soft to very loud.

artiest/van-alexander.text:
Van Alexander was an American bandleader, arranger and composer. He was born in Harlem in 1915 as Alexander Van Vliet Feldman. His mother was a classical pianist and taught him to play the piano. He studied music at Columbia University and was already leading bands and writing arrangements at high school.

In the mid-1930s he sold arrangements to Chick Webb. His best-known work from that time is A-Tisket, A-Tasket, which became a hit for Webb and Ella Fitzgerald and one of her trademarks. He also turned other nursery rhymes into jazz, such as Where, Oh Where Has My Little Dog Gone? and Got a Pebble in My Shoe. In 1938 he started a band of his own, which played in theatres into the 1940s. After that he worked briefly in Larry Clinton's orchestra, before forming a band of his own again in 1942.

Later in the 1940s Bob Crosby brought him to Hollywood. There he worked a great deal as a composer, arranger and conductor of film music. In 1950 he wrote a textbook on film arranging, First Arrangement, and Johnny Mandel was one of his pupils. He wrote music for films with Mickey Rooney, such as The Atomic Kid, for Strait-Jacket and for Tarzan and the Valley of Gold. He also made music for television series such as Bewitched and I Dream of Jeannie and accompanied singers such as Doris Day, Peggy Lee and Dinah Shore. He was twice nominated for an Emmy and received the Henry Mancini Award from ASCAP. He died in 2015, at the age of 100.
artiest/van-alexander.listen: Listen to A-Tisket, A-Tasket by Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald and notice how a nursery rhyme becomes a jazz piece through swinging arrangements.

artiest/van-halen.text:
Van Halen was formed in 1972 in Pasadena, California, by the brothers Eddie and Alex Van Halen. They were born in Amsterdam, the sons of the Dutch musician Jan Van Halen. With singer David Lee Roth and bassist Michael Anthony, Van Halen became one of the biggest hard rock bands of the 1980s. Guitarist Eddie Van Halen was regarded as one of the most influential guitarists of his generation.

The debut album Van Halen was released in February 1978. It contains Eruption, a guitar solo in which Eddie taps the strings with the fingers of his right hand: tapping. That technique was subsequently adopted by countless guitarists. Eddie also played the guitar solo in Michael Jackson's Beat It (1983). On the album 1984 the band took a striking step. Jump was built on a synthesizer riff that Eddie had already written around 1981, but that the rest of the band had rejected at the time. It became Van Halen's only number 1 hit on the Billboard Hot 100. For some of the fans, a keyboard in a hard rock band was treason.

In 1985 Roth left and Sammy Hagar took his place. With him, 5150 (1986) became the band's first album to reach number 1 in America. In 2007 Van Halen was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Eddie Van Halen died in October 2020. Jump showed how rock in the 1980s went along with electronics, like The Final Countdown by Europe two years later.
artiest/van-halen.listen: Jump opens not with a guitar but with a synthesizer riff on an Oberheim OB-Xa, in broad, stabbing chords. Listen to how the song is in C major, and how the guitar solo then enters in a different key, before the synthesizer takes over again.
